Disease combinations, subgroups and interactions

Source: vignettes/interactions.Rmd
interactions.Rmd
library(deconflate)

The distribution of disease combinations

fit_joint() fits the distribution of all 2^n combinations of n diseases, by iterative proportional fitting from independence. The result is the maximum-entropy distribution consistent with the disease probabilities and every association row.

m <- example_supplement()
j <- fit_joint(m)
j
#> <cm_joint> 3 diseases, 8 combinations (exact backend)
#>   Converged: TRUE after 28 sweeps (max residual 8.28e-12)
#>   Association rows: 3
head(combination_probs(j))
#>   d1 d2 d3 n_diseases       prob
#> 1  0  0  0          0 0.64262256
#> 2  0  0  1          1 0.13185683
#> 3  0  1  0          1 0.07737744
#> 4  1  0  0          1 0.06410444
#> 5  0  1  1          2 0.04814317
#> 6  1  1  0          2 0.01589556

Enumerating 2^n combinations limits this exact fit to about 20 diseases. For more, fit_joint(backend = "sampled") fits the same model by Monte Carlo (Gibbs sampling with calibrated parameters, followed by raking to the pairwise tables); deconflate() switches to it by itself above 20 diseases. The sampled backend handles crude pair rows only. See vignette("thresholds-and-scaling") for how it works, its diagnostics and a 24-disease example.

What maximum entropy assumes

With three or more diseases, the probabilities and pairwise associations do not determine a unique distribution: there are 2^n - 1 free probabilities and n(n + 1) / 2 constraints. Maximum entropy picks the one that assumes nothing beyond the rows. It is an assumption, not something the pairwise evidence identifies. With only rows about pairs:

  • the fitted distribution is a log-linear model with all two-way terms and no three-way or higher terms. The odds ratio of a pair is the same whether or not a third disease is present (given the other diseases);
  • three diseases still occur together more (or less) often than under independence, through the pairwise terms;
  • a pair whose association is unknown has no term of its own. Its association is implied by the associations both diseases have with other diseases.

Rows about combinations or subgroups (below) add terms of their own, and the fit matches them too.

Additive results without interactions need only the pairwise tables when every pair has a crude row: then deconflate() uses those tables directly ($diagnostics$method is "pairwise shortcut") and gives the same answer as the full distribution. The distribution matters for unknown pairs, for rows about combinations or subgroups, for interactions, and for event impacts (deconflate(..., event_model = TRUE), which uses the whole distribution; see vignette("event-impacts")).

If the rows cannot hold together, no distribution exists. deconflate() then stops, and check_feasibility() identifies the conflicting pairs:

bad <- cm_population(cm_diseases(c("a", "b", "c"), c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)),
                     cm_associations(c("a", "a", "b"), c("b", "c", "c"), c(20, 20, 0.05)))
check_feasibility(bad, method = "triples")
#> <cm_feasibility> NOT jointly feasible [triples]
#> 
#> Conflicting triples:
#>  disease1 disease2 disease3   gap
#>         a        b        c 0.226

Unknown associations are not independence

A pair without an association row is unknown. Giving it an odds ratio of 1 states that the two diseases are unrelated, which is an assumption of its own. Leaving it unknown lets the maximum-entropy fit imply an association through the other diseases. Here a and c are unrelated in one model and unknown in the other:

d <- cm_diseases(c("a", "b", "c"), c(0.2, 0.3, 0.25))
imp <- cm_impacts(c("a", "b", "c"), c(3, 4, 5), units = "%")
ind <- cm_model(d, imp, associations = cm_associations(c("a", "b", "a"), c("b", "c", "c"), c(3, 2, 1)))
unk <- cm_model(d, imp, associations = cm_associations(c("a", "b"), c("b", "c"), c(3, 2)))
deconflate(ind, n_draws = 0)$adjusted$adjusted
#> [1] 2.263264 2.946945 4.548702
res_unk <- deconflate(unk, n_draws = 0)
res_unk
#> <cm_result> full model [%]
#> 
#>  disease raw adjusted  change
#>        a   3    2.100 -0.3000
#>        b   4    2.987 -0.2532
#>        c   5    4.481 -0.1037
#> 
#> Raw sum: 3.05; adjusted total: 2.436
#> Diagnostics: residual 0.00e+00, condition number 1.7, sign changes 0
#> Unknown pairs: 1 without an association; the fit gave it an odds ratio of 1.19 (see $unknown_pairs).

$unknown_pairs lists the pairs that no row mentions and the odds ratios the fit gave them. Both a and c are positively associated with b, so the fit implies a positive association between them too:

res_unk$unknown_pairs
#>   disease1 disease2 fitted_or
#> 1        a        c  1.194529

The published approximation needs every pair, so compare_methods() reports why it cannot run:

compare_methods(unk)$failed
#>                                                                           published 
#> "The published approximation needs a crude pair row for every pair (missing: a-c)."

Association rows about combinations and subgroups

An association row relates disease (G) to associated_with (H). Either can be a combination of diseases separated by ";"; a combination as the comparison (associated_with) compares animals with all of its diseases to animals with none of them, and a combination as the outcome (disease) is “all of them”. A row can hold within a subgroup (among: "d3", "no d3" or "no others"), and an odds ratio between two diseases can be adjusted for other diseases (adjusted_for). The measures:

measure meaning
OR, RR, RD, phi the 2x2 table of G by H, within among
prevalence P(G | H, among); H may be empty: P(G | among), or the prevalence of a combination
OR_ratio the odds ratio of G and H among among (one disease, S) divided by that among animals without S

The five-disease example has a second LAM-MAS odds ratio (pooled with the first; below), and an OR_ratio row: the LAM-MAS odds ratio is 1.5 times higher among cows with subclinical ketosis (SCK) than among cows without:

ex <- system.file("extdata", "five_diseases", package = "deconflate")
a <- read.csv(file.path(ex, "associations.csv"))
a[, c("disease", "associated_with", "among", "measure", "value", "study")]
#>    disease associated_with among    measure    value   study
#> 1      LAM             MAS               OR 1.800000 Study A
#> 2      LAM             MAS               OR 2.200000 Study B
#> 3      LAM             SCK               OR 2.000000 Study C
#> 4      MET              RP               OR 6.000000 Study D
#> 5      MET             SCK               RR 1.500000 Study E
#> 6      MAS             SCK       prevalence 0.350000 Study F
#> 7      MAS             MET               RD 0.080000 Study G
#> 8      LAM             MET              phi 0.050000 Study H
#> 9       RP             SCK               OR 1.429688 Study I
#> 10     LAM              RP               OR 1.000000        
#> 11     MAS              RP               OR 1.500000 Study J
#> 12     LAM             MAS   SCK   OR_ratio 1.500000 Study K

Pairwise rows cannot identify how often three diseases occur together; an OR_ratio row can. A ratio of 1 is the maximum-entropy assumption. set_three_way() adds or replaces such a row (the ratio is the same whichever disease is the subgroup), and every other row is still matched:

m3 <- set_three_way(m, "d1", "d2", "d3", ratio = 2)
m3$associations
#>   row disease associated_with among adjusted_for  measure value study   source
#> 1   1      d1              d2  <NA>         <NA>       OR     2  <NA>     <NA>
#> 2   2      d1              d3  <NA>         <NA>       OR     1  <NA>     <NA>
#> 3   3      d2              d3  <NA>         <NA>       OR     3  <NA>     <NA>
#> 4   4      d1              d2    d3         <NA> OR_ratio     2  <NA> scenario
#>   note
#> 1 <NA>
#> 2 <NA>
#> 3 <NA>
#> 4 <NA>
j3 <- fit_joint(m3)
c(maximum_entropy = sum(j$prob[rowSums(j$cells) == 3]),
  ratio_2 = sum(j3$prob[rowSums(j3$cells) == 3]))
#> maximum_entropy         ratio_2 
#>     0.008583836     0.010703834

When every pair of the triple has a crude row, the OR_ratio row keeps the pairwise tables fixed, so it changes additive results only through interactions or rows about combinations or subgroups; without them the result is unchanged:

res3 <- deconflate(m3, n_draws = 0)
res3$diagnostics$method
#> [1] "full model"
all.equal(res3$adjusted$adjusted, deconflate(m, n_draws = 0)$adjusted$adjusted)
#> [1] TRUE

It does change results that use the whole distribution, such as event impacts (here hazard ratios of culling, with an overall culling risk of 0.25; see vignette("event-impacts")):

hr <- cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(1.5, 2.0, 1.3), measure = "HR", label = "culling")
e0 <- deconflate(cm_model(m, hr), event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = 0.25, n_draws = 0)
e3 <- deconflate(cm_model(m3, hr), event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = 0.25, n_draws = 0)
rbind(maximum_entropy = setNames(e0$adjusted$adjusted, e0$adjusted$disease),
      ratio_2 = setNames(e3$adjusted$adjusted, e3$adjusted$disease))
#>                       d1       d2       d3
#> maximum_entropy 1.383153 1.890932 1.143987
#> ratio_2         1.379893 1.891328 1.139917

An odds ratio adjusted for other diseases (from a logistic regression) is not the crude odds ratio of the pair. deconflate() matches it as what it is: the coefficient of H in the logistic regression of G on H and the adjustment diseases, within the fitted distribution. Ids in adjusted_for that are not diseases of the model (parity, herd, …) cannot be matched; the row is then used as crude, with a note.

Several rows for one item

Several studies can estimate the same thing. Association rows that fix the same table (the same G, H, among and adjustment) are pooled on the log scale, by random effects (DerSimonian-Laird) by default, or by fixed effect (deconflate(..., pool = "fixed")). A row without a distribution is exact. $heterogeneity gives Cochran’s Q, I^2 and tau^2, and $estimates lists each row with its fitted value:

five <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(ex, "diseases.csv"),
                       associations = file.path(ex, "associations.csv"),
                       impacts = file.path(ex, "impacts_calving_interval.csv"))
res_ci <- deconflate(five, n_draws = 0)
res_ci$heterogeneity
#>          table            item rows k          scale   pooled
#> 1 associations       LAM ~ MAS 1, 2 2 log odds ratio 1.960993
#> 2      impacts all impact rows  all 6          units       NA
#>                   method         Q df         p I2 tau2
#> 1                 random 0.6177079  1 0.4319003  0    0
#> 2 weighted least squares 0.3123068  1 0.5762681  0   NA

With random effects, the draws add the between-study spread (tau^2) to the pooled value. The calving-interval table has two MAS rows (one adjusted for SCK, one crude): impact rows are fitted together by weighted least squares, with weights 1 / SD^2 from their distributions (rows without a distribution are exact):

e <- res_ci$estimates
e[e$table == "impacts", c("row", "item", "adjusted_for", "among", "value", "sd", "fitted", "std_residual")]
#>   row item adjusted_for     among value       sd    fitted std_residual
#> 1   1  LAM         <NA>      <NA>    12 3.000000 12.027295 -0.009098366
#> 2   2  MAS          SCK      <NA>     6 2.000000  6.618529 -0.309264437
#> 3   3  MAS         <NA>      <NA>     9 3.000000  7.603910  0.465363382
#> 4   4  MET         <NA>      <NA>    18 4.463809 18.017756 -0.003977672
#> 5   5  SCK          all      <NA>     4 0.000000  4.000000           NA
#> 6   6   RP         <NA> no others    10 2.526123 10.002042 -0.000808178
res_ci$adjusted
#>   disease    kind raw  adjusted        change rows
#> 1     LAM disease  12 10.206306 -1.494745e-01    1
#> 2     MAS disease  NA  4.768205            NA    2
#> 3     MET disease  18 14.774125 -1.792153e-01    1
#> 4     SCK disease   4  4.000000  2.220446e-16    1
#> 5      RP disease  10 10.002042  2.041557e-04    1

raw is NA for a disease with several rows. The RP row compares cows with RP and no other disease against healthy cows (among = "no others"), which is RP’s own impact.

Impact interactions

An interaction is the extra impact when diseases occur together, in the units of the impact table: positive values are synergistic and negative values antagonistic. Interactions cannot be inferred from associations; they need evidence or explicit scenarios. An impact row about a combination ("d1;d2") adds an interaction term:

  • crude (the default): animals with all of the diseases compared with animals with none of them;
  • adjusted for "all": the interaction itself (the coefficient of the product term in a regression with every disease and term of the model).

set_interaction() adds or replaces a row adjusted for "all":

mi <- set_interaction(m, "d1", "d2", 1)   # 1 percentage point
mi$impacts
#>   row disease among adjusted_for measure value study
#> 1   1      d1  <NA>         <NA>    <NA>   2.5  <NA>
#> 2   2      d2  <NA>         <NA>    <NA>   5.0  <NA>
#> 3   3      d3  <NA>         <NA>    <NA>   7.5  <NA>
#> 4   4   d1;d2  <NA>          all    <NA>   1.0  <NA>
#>                            source note
#> 1 Rasmussen et al. 2022, Table S1 <NA>
#> 2 Rasmussen et al. 2022, Table S1 <NA>
#> 3 Rasmussen et al. 2022, Table S1 <NA>
#> 4                        scenario <NA>
res <- deconflate(mi, n_draws = 0)
res
#> <cm_result> full model; yield [%]
#> 
#>  disease raw adjusted   change
#>       d1 2.5    1.914 -0.23445
#>       d2 5.0    3.241 -0.35187
#>       d3 7.5    6.936 -0.07525
#>    d1;d2 1.0    1.000       NA
#> 
#> Raw sum: 2.5; adjusted total: 2.089; interactions: 0.02448
#> Diagnostics: residual 8.88e-16, condition number 1.6, sign changes 0

The adjusted values reproduce every impact row: the raw values are A %*% adjusted, where each row of A says how much of each term (main impact or interaction) the row’s comparison contains under the fitted distribution:

res$conflation$A
#>                     d1           d2           d3      d1;d2
#> impacts:1 1.000000e+00 1.053266e-01 2.058839e-11 0.24479393
#> impacts:2 7.434818e-02 1.000000e+00 2.096236e-01 0.16319595
#> impacts:3 1.158099e-11 1.670438e-01 1.000000e+00 0.02304974
#> impacts:4 0.000000e+00 2.038632e-16 0.000000e+00 1.00000000
as.vector(res$conflation$A %*% res$adjusted$adjusted)
#> [1] 2.5 5.0 7.5 1.0
res$estimates$value[res$estimates$table == "impacts"]
#> [1] 2.5 5.0 7.5 1.0

A simulated herd with known impacts (2, 4 and 6 percent) and interactions (1 point for d1 with d2, 1.5 for d2 with d3) checks the method. By default simulate_raw_impacts() simulates a crude row for each disease and each combination:

raw <- simulate_raw_impacts(m, c(d1 = 2, d2 = 4, d3 = 6),
                            interactions = c("d1;d2" = 1, "d2;d3" = 1.5))
raw[, c("disease", "adjusted_for", "value")]
#>   disease adjusted_for     value
#> 1      d1         <NA>  2.714619
#> 2      d2         <NA>  6.136904
#> 3      d3         <NA>  7.116677
#> 4   d1;d2         <NA>  8.608404
#> 5   d2;d3         <NA> 11.772543
deconflate(cm_model(m, raw), n_draws = 0)$adjusted
#>   disease        kind       raw adjusted     change rows
#> 1      d1     disease  2.714619      2.0 -0.2632484    1
#> 2      d2     disease  6.136904      4.0 -0.3482055    1
#> 3      d3     disease  7.116677      6.0 -0.1569099    1
#> 4   d1;d2 interaction  8.608404      1.0         NA    1
#> 5   d2;d3 interaction 11.772543      1.5         NA    1

The interaction terms of the model are the combinations that appear in the disease column. The rows must tell the terms apart: there must be at least as many independent rows as terms (one per disease and per combination); otherwise deconflate() stops and names the terms the rows do not determine. Any row that depends on the interaction helps to determine it: besides a row for the combination itself, e.g. the impact of d1 among animals with d2 (among = "d2"), set against that of d1 overall.

The welfare table of the five-disease example has two interactions adjusted for all, and a crude LAM;SCK row whose value implies an antagonistic LAM:SCK interaction:

welfare <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(ex, "diseases.csv"),
                          associations = file.path(ex, "associations.csv"),
                          impacts = file.path(ex, "impacts_welfare.csv"))
res_w <- deconflate(welfare, n_draws = 0)
res_w$adjusted
#>   disease        kind  raw   adjusted     change rows
#> 1     LAM     disease 10.0  8.7442977 -0.1255702    1
#> 2     MAS     disease  6.0  3.8319918 -0.3613347    1
#> 3     MET     disease  5.0  3.1977586 -0.3604483    1
#> 4     SCK     disease  3.0  1.0855585 -0.6381472    1
#> 5      RP     disease  4.0  2.1515488 -0.4621128    1
#> 6 LAM;MAS interaction  2.0  2.0000000         NA    1
#> 7  MET;RP interaction  1.5  1.5000000         NA    1
#> 8 LAM;SCK interaction 11.5 -0.6200834         NA    1
res_w$totals
#>    raw_sum adjusted_total interaction_total
#> 1 5.845091       4.147957         0.1398854

For a term with one row, raw is that row’s value. For a crude combination row it is the difference between animals with both diseases and animals with neither, which includes both main impacts: 11.5 points for LAM;SCK, which the model splits into the main impacts of LAM and SCK and an interaction of about -0.6.

For event impacts, a combination row adds an interaction on the log-hazard scale (the culling table of the five-disease example has one); see vignette("event-impacts").

Attribution

The expected aggregate is sum_i p_i b_i + sum_T P(all of T) delta_T over the interaction terms T. Removing any disease of a term removes that term, so each disease’s Shapley value is its own term plus an equal share of every interaction term it is involved in. This is the contributions table:

attribute_burden(res)
#>   disease      main interaction     total      share
#> 1      d1 0.1913880   0.0122397 0.2036277 0.09747208
#> 2      d2 0.4860961   0.0122397 0.4983358 0.23854231
#> 3      d3 1.3871243   0.0000000 1.3871243 0.66398561

For general loss functions, shapley_by_cell() computes Shapley values cell by cell over the joint distribution. For example, with proportional impacts that compound (here as proportions):

shapley_by_cell(j, loss_multiplicative(c(d1 = 0.02, d2 = 0.04, d3 = 0.06)))
#>   disease     shapley      share
#> 1      d1 0.001978346 0.09981218
#> 2      d2 0.005922273 0.29879258
#> 3      d3 0.011920065 0.60139525

Which interactions or three-way associations would matter?

screen_interactions() sets an interaction of each size for each pair in turn and reports the change in the aggregate and in the ranking of diseases; screen_three_way() does the same with an OR_ratio row for each triple. Without interactions, three-way rows change additive results only through unknown pairs:

screen_interactions(m, values = c(-1, 1))
#> <cm_screen> 6 scenarios; baseline total 2.109
#>   pair      status   scenario total  change rel_change max_rank_shift rank_corr
#>  d2:d3 interaction delta = -1  2.15  0.0383    0.01815              0         1
#>  d2:d3 interaction  delta = 1  2.07 -0.0383   -0.01815              0         1
#>  d1:d3 interaction  delta = 1  2.09 -0.0209   -0.00990              0         1
#>  d1:d3 interaction delta = -1  2.13  0.0209    0.00990              0         1
#>  d1:d2 interaction  delta = 1  2.09 -0.0201   -0.00955              0         1
#>  d1:d2 interaction delta = -1  2.13  0.0201    0.00955              0         1
#>  failed
#>    <NA>
#>    <NA>
#>    <NA>
#>    <NA>
#>    <NA>
#>    <NA>
screen_three_way(m, ratios = c(0.5, 2))
#> <cm_screen> 2 scenarios; baseline total 2.109
#>      pair    status    scenario total    change rel_change max_rank_shift
#>  d1:d2:d3 three-way   ratio = 2  2.11 -6.91e-10  -3.28e-10              0
#>  d1:d2:d3 three-way ratio = 0.5  2.11  1.35e-10   6.40e-11              0
#>  rank_corr failed
#>          1   <NA>
#>          1   <NA>
screen_three_way(mi, ratios = c(0.5, 2))
#> <cm_screen> 2 scenarios; baseline total 2.089
#>      pair    status    scenario total   change rel_change max_rank_shift
#>  d1:d2:d3 three-way   ratio = 2  2.09 -0.00234   -0.00112              0
#>  d1:d2:d3 three-way ratio = 0.5  2.09  0.00231    0.00111              0
#>  rank_corr failed
#>          1   <NA>
#>          1   <NA>
